endorsements.quote: Physicians should recognize that medical LLMs function best when used adjunctively to validate evidence-based practice, rather than to generate novel treatments or be allowed to operate autonomously.

Physicians should understand the mechanism underlying LLMs; their intrinsic limitations and vulnerabilities; the impact of prompt engineering on output quality; and how to reduce hallucinatory behavior.
Physicians should understand how privacy and confidentiality may be breached by incautious use of public LLM models.

unlisted_practices: Physicians should demand dataset provenance and performance metrics from software vendors before AI models are introduced into the clinic.
Integrate AI education into standard medical curricula.
Increase physician participation in the development, validation, and implementation of clinical AI systems, tailored to local deployments.
Physicians should collaborate with clinical informaticians throughout clinical AI implementation to ensure regulatory preparedness and compliance.
Domain-specific consultative LLMs should offer system prompt customization as an option.
Physicians should understand the custody and retention issues of source recordings generated by ambient AI scribes.
Fund research initiatives exploring optimal physician-AI collaboration, including practitioner proficiency in customizing LLM tools.
Clinical practitioners should avoid defaulting to passive acceptance of AI integrated into institutionally procured software.
Physicians should understand whether information generated by LLMs will be exported and used for training purposes.
Physicians should be able to educate ancillary health care staff on proper AI use and instill patient confidence in responsible AI deployment.

screen.reason: Commentary discussing the impact of generative AI and LLMs on clinical practice, physician roles, and liability, advocating for AI education in standard medical curricula.
